prediction, click AUC and search depth. The direction of that shift is what theory
predicts, because a correctly specified structural model buys efficiency and the value
of efficiency falls as data accumulate. A benchmark trained directly on purchase
cross-entropy should also be hardest to beat on exactly that loss. We report it because a
margin that flips with the split is not a margin to build a claim on. The robust part
of claim 4 in our replication is the advantage on sequence-level quantities, where the
benchmark has no mechanism at all, and the policy results below.

**Does not separate.** Two of the three policy experiments. On ranking and on
new-product targeting, the deep benchmark matches SST. Both experiments rearrange
objects the benchmark has a coefficient for, and both require only that a model order
preferences correctly within a session, which the shared encoder does equally well in
either model. A replication that ran only those two experiments would conclude that
the structural half of the model is unnecessary. The separation appears in the
forecasting exercise of @sec-dss-policy-rank and, decisively, in
@sec-dss-policy-cost.

**Cannot be assessed.** Everything specific to the paper's data. Magnitudes of search
costs in a real category, the shape of real cross-session preference dynamics, the
size of the revenue gains on the firm's actual traffic, and whether the identifying
exclusion holds on that site. A simulation can establish that a method recovers a
truth. It cannot establish that a particular estimate describes the world.

**Estimation caveats that generalize.** Two are worth carrying into any project of
this kind. The smoothing temperature trades two biases against each other and has an
interior optimum that depends on the draw budget and on the size of the model, so it
must be calibrated by Monte Carlo, per @sec-dss-montecarlo. And a fitted structural
model evaluating its own preferred policy is over-optimistic, so counterfactual gains
should be reported as upper bounds unless they are validated against held-out policy
variation. @sec-dss-policy-cost over-states the revenue gain from halving search costs
by about sixty percent while getting the sign and the order of magnitude right, which
is roughly the accuracy this class of exercise delivers at this sample size.

## Scaling Up {#sec-dss-scaling}

Everything above is base R with hand-derived gradients, which is the right choice for
a chapter whose purpose is to make the mechanism inspectable. It is the wrong choice
for a project. At realistic scale, use automatic differentiation and mini-batching,
and keep the structural layer exactly as it is written here. The sketch below is the
same model in `torch`, which is the stable choice in R because it links to libtorch
directly and needs no Python installation.

```{r}
#| label: dss-torch-sketch
#| eval: false
library(torch)

# The Weitzman layer. Only the inversion needs a custom derivative, and it is
# available in closed form from @eq-dss-dmdc, so autograd handles everything else.
resv_layer <- autograd_function(
  forward = function(ctx, cc) {
    m <- torch_tensor(resv_m(as.numeric(cc$cpu())))$view_as(cc)
    ctx$save_for_backward(m = m)
    m
  },
  backward = function(ctx, grad_output) {
    m <- ctx$saved_variables$m
    # dm/dc = -1 / (1 - Phi(m))
    list(cc = grad_output * (-1 / (1 - torch_special_ndtr(m))))
  }
)

sst_module <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(d_emb, d_ff, n_att, n_lin, n_head = 4) {
    self$emb  <- nn_linear(n_att, d_emb, bias = FALSE)
    self$attn <- nn_multihead_attention(d_emb, n_head, batch_first = TRUE)
    self$ff   <- nn_sequential(nn_linear(d_emb, d_ff), nn_relu(),
                               nn_linear(d_ff, d_emb))
    self$norm <- nn_layer_norm(d_emb)
    self$alpha <- nn_linear(n_lin, 1, bias = FALSE)
    self$gam   <- nn_parameter(torch_tensor(c(-4, 0.1)))
    self$lam   <- nn_parameter(torch_tensor(0.1))
    self$lsig  <- nn_parameter(torch_tensor(log(0.7)))
  },
  forward = function(x_item, x_hist, mask_hist, slot) {
    e_h <- self$emb(x_hist)
    h   <- self$attn(e_h[, 1:1, ], e_h, e_h, key_padding_mask = mask_hist)[[1]]
    h   <- self$norm(h + self$ff(h))
    e_j <- self$emb(x_item)
    list(dbar = self$alpha(x_item)$squeeze(-1) +
                torch_einsum("bjd,bod->bj", list(e_j, h)),
         m    = resv_layer(torch_exp(self$gam[1] + self$gam[2] * slot)),
         e    = e_j)
  }
)
```

Three practical notes for that implementation. Mini-batch over sessions and keep the
simulation draws fixed within a batch, so the objective a batch sees is deterministic.
Anneal the smoothing temperature downward only while increasing the number of draws,
guided by the diagnostic of @sec-dss-montecarlo. And carry the likelihood's inequality
loop as a masked tensor operation over search steps, which is what the R code above
does with matrices and is the only part that needs care to vectorize.

## Using This as a Model Paper {#sec-dss-template}

The reason to study SST closely is that almost nothing in it is about search. Strip
the application away and a template remains. It applies wherever a behavioral theory
produces a decision rule and a firm holds rich individual-level data.

**One.** Find the place where the economic model asks for a primitive the analyst
cannot observe. In sequential search it is the pre-search expected utility. In a
dynamic durable-goods model it is the expected flow utility. In a learning model it is
the prior. Classical practice fills that slot with a linear index because it must, and
the linear index is usually the least defended part of the model.

**Two.** Put a network in that slot, and only in that slot. The economics stays
untouched. The test of a deep structural model is whether the theory would still be
recognizable if the network were replaced by a linear index, and whether that
replacement nests as a restriction. Here it does, exactly, which is what makes the
ablation in @sec-dss-prediction interpretable.

**Three.** Make the decision rule differentiable, and prefer a rule whose derivative
you can write down. @eq-dss-dmdc is the whole reason the SST trains. It exists because
Weitzman's equation has a clean implicit derivative. When the rule is a
maximum or an ordering, rewrite the observed event as a product of pairwise
comparisons and smooth each one, as in @eq-dss-event.

**Four.** State identification in terms of functions. Name the
normalizations. Name the exclusion restriction, and be explicit that it is an
assumption about the world. Then show which margin of the data identifies which
object, as in the three lemmas of @sec-dss-identification.

**Five.** Validate against a known truth before validating against a benchmark. The
temperature pathology in @sec-dss-montecarlo is invisible in fit statistics and fatal
to every estimate. A deep structural model has enough moving parts that a Monte Carlo
where the truth lies inside the model class is not optional.

**Six.** Report counterfactuals as the deliverable, and report the forecast alongside
the choice. Picking the better of two policies is a weak test that a flexible
predictor often passes. Forecasting what a policy will deliver, and answering about
an intervention with no coefficient in the reduced form, is the test structure is for.

## Key Takeaways

- Sequential search theory supplies a decision rule whose central object, the
  reservation utility of @weitzman1979optimal, is a monotone and differentiable
  function of the pre-search index and the search cost. That differentiability is
  what lets economics sit inside a neural network as an ordinary layer.
- The SST of @song2026sst puts a transformer in the one slot where the classical
  search model was guessing: the map from a consumer's cross-session history to the
  utility they expect before clicking. Setting the deep components to zero recovers
  the classical model exactly, so the deep structure is a testable extension.
- Identification in a deep structural model applies to functions. Under a
  scale and location normalization and the exclusion of slot position from utility,
  choice identifies the pre-search index, search order identifies differences in
  reservation cutoffs, and stopping identifies their level. The network weights are
  not identified and nothing of interest depends on them.
- The differentiable likelihood requires smoothing a product of indicator functions.
  The smoothing temperature must be chosen jointly with the number of simulation
  draws. Too low a temperature produces a silent collapse of every coefficient
  toward zero, diagnosable without knowing the truth by checking whether the
  objective is stable as draws are added.
- In our replication the deep components make the structural parameters estimable.
  The classical model mis-estimates the search-cost function because preference
  heterogeneity it cannot represent is absorbed into the search process.
- Against a deep benchmark of equal capacity the structural model is ahead on
  prediction, by a wide margin on search depth and by a thin and sample-sensitive
  margin on purchase. Its decisive advantage lies elsewhere. Choosing between layouts
  is something a flexible predictor does just as well, because it needs only the
  ordering of preferences. Forecasting what a layout will earn, and answering about an
  intervention that has no coefficient in the reduced form at all, is what the
  structural half of the model is for.
